description: We are 4 friends from the Arab Academy for Science and Technology in the main branch in Alexandria. We share a common love for all things robotics and AI, and ofcourse Space!
summary:
Dalil Mars is an autonomous surface navigation engine, glove-compatible astronaut EVA tablet terminal, and planetary GIS ground control station for Jezero Crater, Mars. We integrated authentic orbital datasets including USGS SIM 3464 geologic maps, MRO CTX 20-meter stereo elevation models, ESA HRSC relief, and THEMIS thermal inertia with live NASA Mars 2020 Perseverance telemetry, MEDA weather feeds, and Mastcam-Z gigapixel 360-degree panoramas. This powers a sub-millisecond Hierarchical Corridor A* (HC-A*) pathfinding engine that navigates around 60-meter sheer cliffs, treacherous sand dunes, and communication blackouts.

Without GPS satellites, paved roads, or breathable air, traversing the Martian surface is an unforgiving survival challenge. Dalil Mars transforms complex planetary cartography into an intuitive interplanetary survival guide. It calculates metabolic oxygen and battery consumption against Martian gravity (3.72 m/s²), predicts topographic solar shadows, and strictly enforces the Apollo/Artemis Rule #1 walkback horizon to ensure astronauts never exceed their life-support return limits. During sudden dust storms or suit emergencies, it automatically generates instant abort vectors to the nearest habitat, ensuring every explorer makes it back alive.
details:
Dalil Mars operates as an integrated surface navigation and mission support platform designed for human astronaut extravehicular activities and autonomous robotic rovers in Jezero Crater. At its foundation, the system processes raw planetary datasets through a modular six-stage Python pipeline utilizing GDAL, Rasterio, and NumPy. This pipeline mosaics high-resolution 20.2-meter-per-pixel Digital Terrain Models from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX and Mars Express HRSC stereoscopic data, cross-referencing them with the USGS SIM 3464 geologic geodatabase. The pipeline identifies treacherous features such as 20 to 60 meter vertical delta scarps, boulder fields, and active sand dunes, transforming these into rasterized slope grids, cost surfaces, and a precomputed four-dimensional all-pairs macro-heuristic tensor. At runtime, a FastAPI backend runs a hierarchical corridor A* pathfinding algorithm that navigates this high-resolution mesh. The engine models authentic Martian physical dynamics, factoring in 3.72 meters per second squared surface gravity, asymmetric mechanical climb work during ascents, Allison-McEwen solar ephemeris, Beer-Lambert atmospheric dust extinction, and ray-marched terrain shadows that affect solar power and spacesuit heating. Additionally, it ray-marches 437 megahertz radio line-of-sight across 3D topography to detect communication blackout corridors relative to Hab Alpha and regional relay masts.

The system continuously models life support consumption by tracking metabolic oxygen rates and battery reserves based on suit mass, locomotion speed, and payload loadouts, whether on foot in an xEMU spacesuit or operating an electric mule rover. To ensure crew safety, the engine integrates an Apollo and Artemis walkback horizon calculator that tracks the point of no return to the nearest pressurized habitat, automatically rerouting through intermediate charging and oxygen pit-stops whenever projected reserves breach mandatory 15 percent safety thresholds. The frontend, constructed using React 18, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, provides distinct user interfaces suited for different mission roles. Astronauts interact with a 2D Leaflet tactical map supporting custom exclusion zone rasterization, a Three.js WebGL 3D terrain viewer for spatial elevation inspection, an interactive 360-degree Mastcam-Z gigapixel panoramic viewer, and a 110-degree field-of-view Visor Augmented Reality heads-up display synchronized in real time via the browser BroadcastChannel API. Mission controllers utilize a dedicated Ground Control operations console to monitor telemetry, draw hazardous exclusion polygons, and optimize multi-waypoint science tours.

Development of the project relied on Python 3.10+, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3, leveraging FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, and Pydantic on the backend, alongside React, Vite, Leaflet, Three.js, and Lucide React on the frontend. Hardware considerations included compatibility with virtual and augmented reality headsets such as the Meta Quest via WebXR, as well as tablet configurations built for pressurized extravehicular glove interactions. During engineering, our team carefully evaluated human factors, operational spaceflight constraints, and Martian planetary science. The user interface incorporates high-contrast styling and enlarged 48 to 56 pixel touch targets to remain operable through gold-tinted helmet visors and bulky pressurized gloves. Recognizing the four to twenty-four minute communication latency between Earth and Mars, all pathfinding and life-support calculations run locally at the edge with zero cloud dependencies. Furthermore, the cartography integrates thermal inertia data from 2001 Mars Odyssey THEMIS to distinguish solid, load-bearing bedrock from treacherous loose dust mantles, while Mars 2020 MEDA atmospheric measurements dictate dynamic speed and thermal degradation factors.

The creativity of Dalil Mars lies in fusing macro-scale orbital remote sensing with micro-scale tactical surface survival. By coupling coarse precomputed heuristic tensors with fine-grained ray-marching, the engine resolves complex, physics-constrained paths across millions of terrain pixels in sub-second execution times without compromising accuracy. The primary benefit of this system is that it replaces dangerous straight-line waypoint navigation with an intelligent, physics-informed traversal model that guarantees life-support margins, avoids impassable drop-offs, and ensures active communications coverage. The intended impact is to de-risk human surface operations on Mars, providing future Artemis and Mars expedition crews with the spatial awareness and real-time autonomy needed to conduct high-priority scientific research while ensuring every astronaut returns safely to habitat.
